lesson.title: Four-Part Writing
lesson.summary: Soprano, alto, tenor and bass: how to space, double and connect chords so that every voice sings its own line.

section.title: Four voices
section.p: Harmony is traditionally taught in four parts, named after the voices of a choir: soprano, alto, tenor and bass. Each voice is a melody of its own, and each stays in a comfortable range. The ranges used here follow Kostka and Payne:

list.li: Soprano: C4 to G5.
Alto: G3 to C5.
Tenor: C3 to G4.
Bass: E2 to C4.

section.p: Four-part music is written on the grand staff: soprano and alto on the treble staff, tenor and bass on the bass staff. Usually each voice has its own stem direction, up for soprano and tenor, down for alto and bass; the examples in these lessons show the two voices of each staff as one chord.
Three rules keep the voices apart:

list.li: Spacing: no more than an octave between soprano and alto, or between alto and tenor. Tenor and bass may be further apart.
No crossing: a lower voice never sounds above a higher one, for example the alto above the soprano.
No overlap: a voice does not move past the note that a neighbouring voice has just sung.

figure.caption: A C major triad in close position, with soprano and tenor less than an octave apart, then in open position. In the third chord the soprano and alto are more than an octave apart: a spacing error.

check.prompt: Between which voices may the distance be more than an octave?
check.explanation: The upper voices should stay within an octave of each other, so soprano–alto and alto–tenor are at most an octave apart. The bass is free: a wide gap between bass and tenor sounds natural, because the overtones of low notes fill it.

section.title: Doubling
section.p: A triad has three notes and four-part writing four voices, so one note is doubled, sung by two voices. The usual choices:

list.li: Root-position triads: double the root. The fifth may be left out, with the root tripled; the third is never left out.
First-inversion triads: any note may be doubled that gives good voice leading, except the leading tone.
Second-inversion triads: double the bass, the fifth of the chord.
Diminished triads, such as vii°6 and ii°6: double the third, which is usually the bass.

callout.p: Never double a tendency tone: the leading tone or the seventh of a chord. Both have to resolve in one direction, and two voices resolving the same way would move in parallel octaves.

check.prompt: In C major, which note of the V chord G–B–D must not be doubled?
check.explanation: B is the leading tone of C major. It tends to rise to C; doubled, both voices would either rise in parallel octaves or one would have to leave the tendency unresolved. Doubling the root G is the normal choice.

section.title: Motion between voices
section.p: Any two voices move in one of four ways:

list.li: Parallel motion: both move in the same direction and keep the same interval number between them, for example a third.
Similar motion: both move in the same direction, but the interval between them changes.
Contrary motion: they move in opposite directions.
Oblique motion: one voice stays on its note while the other moves.

figure.caption: Parallel thirds, similar motion from a third to a fifth, contrary motion from a fourth to a sixth, and oblique motion with the lower voice holding E4.

section.p: Contrary and oblique motion keep the voices most independent. Good four-part writing mixes all four kinds, with plenty of contrary motion between the bass and the soprano.

check.prompt: The soprano rises a step while the bass falls a fifth. What kind of motion is this?
check.explanation: The voices move in opposite directions, so the motion is contrary, however large each step. In similar motion both voices go the same way; in oblique motion one of them stays.

section.title: Parallel fifths and octaves
section.p: Two voices that move from a perfect fifth to another perfect fifth, or from an octave or unison to another, make parallel fifths or parallel octaves. They are avoided in common-practice part writing, because the two voices blend so well that they stop sounding independent. Compound intervals count too: a twelfth moving to a twelfth is a parallel fifth.

figure.caption: IV–V in C major. When every voice rises, the tenor and bass move in parallel octaves and the soprano and tenor in parallel fifths. Moving the upper voices down, against the bass, avoids both.

list.li: Contrary fifths and octaves, a perfect fifth or octave followed by another in contrary motion, are also avoided in four-part writing.
A perfect fifth followed by a diminished fifth is acceptable. A diminished fifth followed by a perfect fifth is acceptable too, as long as the bass is not one of the two voices.

Direct fifths and octaves, also called hidden fifths and octaves, arise when the soprano and bass reach a perfect fifth or octave in similar motion. They are avoided when the soprano leaps; with a step in the soprano they are acceptable.

check.prompt: Which two voices move in parallel fifths here?

figure.description: Two four-part chords on a grand staff. The bass and tenor both rise one step; the alto rises one step and the soprano falls a third.

check.explanation: The tenor moves from G3 to A3 while the bass moves from C3 to D3: a perfect fifth followed by another perfect fifth. The soprano moves from two octaves above the bass to a twelfth, in contrary motion, which is fine.

section.title: Resolving tendency tones
section.p: Two notes have a strong pull that four-part writing respects:

list.li: The leading tone rises to the tonic, especially in the soprano or the bass. In an inner voice in V–I it may instead fall a third to degree 5, so that the tonic chord is complete.
The seventh of a chord resolves down by step: in V7–I, degree 4 falls to degree 3.

section.p: When both tendencies resolve, V7 and I cannot both be complete. Either a complete V7 resolves to an incomplete I, with a tripled root and no fifth, or an incomplete V7, with a doubled root and no fifth, resolves to a complete I.

figure.caption: V7–I in C major, twice. In both, B rises to C and the seventh F falls to E. The first V7 is complete and its I has three Cs; the second V7 leaves out D and its I is complete.

check.prompt: How does the seventh of V7 normally move when the chord resolves to I?
check.option: It stays on the same note
check.explanation: The chordal seventh is a dissonance that resolves down by step: in C major, F falls to E, the third of I. Only the leading tone rises.

section.title: Writing a progression step by step

step.p: The key is G major and the soprano is given: G4, G4, F#4, G4. Write the bass first, on the roots: G2, C3, D3, G2.
Fill in the first chord: the root is doubled by bass and soprano, so alto and tenor take the fifth and the third, D4 and B3.
Move to IV. Keep the common tone G in the soprano, and move the other voices to the nearest notes of C–E–G: the alto from D4 up to E4, the tenor from B3 up to C4.

IV and V share no notes, and the bass rises a step. Move the upper voices down, against the bass, to the nearest notes of V: the alto to D4, the tenor to A3. The soprano has the leading tone, F#4; check that it is not doubled.

Resolve to I: the leading tone rises to G4, the alto keeps the common tone D4, and the tenor rises to B3. Finally, check every pair of voices for parallel fifths and octaves, and every chord for spacing and range.

callout.p: Two habits solve most problems: keep common tones in the same voice, and when the bass moves by step, move the upper voices in the opposite direction.

check.prompt: Going from I to IV in C major, which note can stay in the same voice?
check.explanation: I is C–E–G and IV is F–A–C. Their common tone is C, which can be held while the other voices move to F and A.
